patient.name: Grace Mensah
patient.setting: GP surgery, then the Emergency Department
patient.complaint: Four months of exhaustion, dizziness on standing and weight loss
background: Vitiligo on her hands since her twenties
No regular steroids, inhaled or oral

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' with fatigue, weight loss, postural hypotension, hyperpigmentation and low sodium with high potassium. Distractors: hypothyroidism, secondary adrenal insufficiency (no pigmentation), SIADH, Conn's. Addisonian crisis is the emergency version.

points: Grace, 34: tired all the time for 4 months.
Lost 5 kg; nauseated; vague tummy ache.
Light-headed when she stands; **craves crisps and salt**.
Her partner says she looks **tanned** though it is winter.

steps.lead: Grace has the classic picture: fatigue, weight loss, **postural hypotension**, nausea, abdominal pain and **salt craving**.

points: Dark **palmar creases** and dark patches inside her cheeks.

steps.lead: Her pigmented creases and buccal mucosa mean **high ACTH**, so this is **primary** adrenal failure, not pituitary.

steps.title: Grace's U&Es and glucose
steps.text: Low sodium, high potassium and a raised urea (volume depletion): the electrolyte fingerprint of aldosterone deficiency.

visual.title: Serum potassium
visual.label: Grace 5.9
visual.caption: High K with low Na points to Addison's; Conn's is the mirror image (low K, high Na).

steps.lead: Grace lacks **cortisol and aldosterone**: the zona fasciculata and zona glomerulosa have both failed, so this is **primary** adrenal insufficiency.

steps.q: Grace has vitiligo and hypothyroidism. What is the most likely cause of her Addison's?
steps.r: **Autoimmune adrenalitis** causes 80–90% of cases and clusters with thyroid disease, vitiligo and type 1 diabetes.

steps.lead: With two other autoimmune diseases, Grace almost certainly has **autoimmune adrenalitis**. In someone from a TB area, think **TB adrenalitis**.
Grace's real danger is **Addisonian crisis**: an infection or a missed dose can tip her into shock, hypoglycaemia and hyperkalaemia.

steps.text: Hypoglycaemia is **common** in adrenal crisis. In a collapsed patient with low BP, low glucose and high K, think adrenal crisis, not just sepsis.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?' (9am cortisol) and 'Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?' (short Synacthen test). Watch the cut-offs: 100–500 nmol/L is inconclusive; 30-minute cortisol ≥450 is normal.

steps.q: The GP suspects adrenal insufficiency. What is the first blood test?
steps.r: A **9am cortisol** is timed to the diurnal peak. An afternoon cortisol is naturally low and misleading.

steps.lead: Grace's 9am cortisol is **140 nmol/L**: low, but in the **100–500** grey zone, so she needs a short Synacthen test.

visual.title: 9am cortisol
visual.label: Grace 140
visual.caption: Grace is in the grey zone: the short Synacthen test decides.

steps.lead: The **short Synacthen test** confirms it: IM/IV synthetic ACTH, then cortisol at 30 minutes. A normal response is **≥450 nmol/L**.

visual.title: Grace's short Synacthen test
visual.caption: Grace's adrenals cannot respond to ACTH: **primary adrenal insufficiency** confirmed.

steps.title: Follow-up tests
steps.text: High ACTH and renin with positive adrenal antibodies: autoimmune primary adrenal failure.

steps.lead: Further tests find the level and cause: the **prolonged ACTH stimulation test** separates primary, secondary and tertiary, with **autoantibodies** and **adrenal imaging**.

steps.text: Never delay treatment in a shocked patient to do a Synacthen test. Take a cortisol sample, then give **hydrocortisone** straight away.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?' for a collapsed patient (IV/IM hydrocortisone 100 mg plus 0.9% saline) and long-term questions: hydrocortisone plus fludrocortisone, and sick day rules (double hydrocortisone, same fludrocortisone).

steps.q: Grace is diagnosed. Which combination replaces what she has lost?
steps.r: **Hydrocortisone** replaces cortisol; **fludrocortisone** replaces aldosterone. Spironolactone blocks aldosterone and would worsen her potassium.

steps.lead: Grace takes **hydrocortisone** in split doses, most in the **morning**, to copy the natural diurnal rhythm, plus daily **fludrocortisone**.

visual.title: Hydrocortisone dosing copies the cortisol rhythm
visual.caption: Largest dose on waking, smaller doses at midday and afternoon, none late at night.

steps.lead: Grace learns the **sick day rules**: if her temperature is **above 37.5°C**, she **doubles hydrocortisone**, keeps fludrocortisone the same, and uses her **IM injection kit** if vomiting.

steps.text: Every patient gets a **steroid emergency card**, a MedicAlert bracelet and an IM hydrocortisone kit.

points: Eight months later: norovirus; she has **vomited** all night.
She could not keep her tablets down.
Brought in drowsy and pale; abdominal pain.

steps.title: ED bloods
steps.text: Shock, hypoglycaemia and hyperkalaemia in a known Addison's patient: **adrenal crisis**.

o: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg and IV 0.9% saline
steps.r: **Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV/IM immediately** plus large-volume **0.9% saline**. She cannot absorb oral tablets, and the steroid also lowers her potassium.

steps.lead: Any Addison's patient who is unwell and collapses is treated as an **adrenal crisis**: Grace gets **hydrocortisone 100 mg IV** and fast **0.9% saline**.

steps.title: Adrenal crisis in the ED
nodes: Suspect: known Addison's or steroid user, unwell, low BP
steps.caption: Never wait for tests before the hydrocortisone.

steps.lead: Grace's crisis plan follows **Society for Endocrinology** emergency guidance; her long-term care follows **NICE CKS: Addison's disease**.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why there is hyperpigmentation (ACTH and MSH share POMC), why sodium falls and potassium rises (aldosterone deficiency in the distal nephron), and why stress triggers a crisis.

steps.title: Why Grace became unwell
nodes: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex
Aldosterone loss → Na lost, K kept

steps.lead: Grace's autoantibodies slowly destroyed her **whole cortex**, so she lost both **cortisol and aldosterone**.
Grace's tan is **ACTH**: it is cut from **POMC**, the same precursor as **MSH**, which stimulates melanocytes.

steps.q: Why is a patient with secondary adrenal insufficiency not pigmented?
steps.r: In pituitary failure **ACTH is low**, so there is no excess POMC product to darken the skin.

steps.lead: Without aldosterone, Grace's distal nephron cannot reabsorb **sodium** or excrete **potassium**: low Na, high K and a contracted volume.
Cortisol keeps vessels responsive to **catecholamines**. With norovirus and no stress-dose steroid, Grace's vessels could not hold her BP.

steps.text: Sick day rules copy the **cortisol surge** a normal adrenal makes in illness. Fixed doses cannot do that on their own.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of Addison's disease in the UK?
What electrolyte pattern is typical of Addison's disease?
Which sign distinguishes primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency?
mcq.r: **Hyperpigmentation** (from high ACTH) occurs only in primary disease.

mcq.q: What is the initial investigation for suspected Addison's?
mcq.r: A **9am cortisol**, at the diurnal peak.

mcq.q: What is the immediate treatment of adrenal crisis?
o: IV dexamethasone after the Synacthen test

mcq.q: What are the sick day rules in Addison's?
Why does hyperpigmentation occur in Addison's?
o: ACTH and MSH share the precursor POMC
mcq.r: Raised **ACTH** comes from **POMC**, which also makes MSH.

prompts.q: What is Addison's disease and which hormones are lost?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: primary means the gland itself, so both hormones go.
Exam thinking: autoimmune unless the stem says TB, cancer, HIV or sepsis.

points.p: Associations: thyroid disease, vitiligo, type 1 diabetes

prompts.q: What are the symptoms, signs and biochemistry of Addison's?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the stem is vague until the electrolytes arrive.

points.why: Salt craving is a strong clue.

prompts.q: How do you tell primary from secondary adrenal insufficiency?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: look at the skin and the potassium.

points.p: Secondary keeps aldosterone, so potassium is normal

prompts.q: What is an Addisonian crisis, what triggers it, and what is Waterhouse-Friderichsen?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: collapsed + low glucose + high K = crisis.

points.p: Triggers: infection, trauma, surgery, missed steroids
Waterhouse-Friderichsen: meningococcal sepsis, bilateral adrenal haemorrhage

prompts.q: How do you investigate suspected Addison's, with cut-offs?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: initial 9am cortisol; confirm with Synacthen.

points.p: Then: prolonged ACTH test, autoantibodies, adrenal imaging

prompts.q: What is the long-term treatment of Addison's and the sick day rules?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: replace both hormones; double only hydrocortisone.

points.p: Hydrocortisone, most of the dose in the morning
Vomiting: IM hydrocortisone kit until it stops

prompts.q: How do you manage an adrenal crisis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: treat first, test later.

points.why: Do not wait for cortisol results.

points.p: Any known Addison's patient who collapses = adrenal crisis

prompts.q: Why do patients with Addison's get pigmentation, low sodium and high potassium?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: two hormones, two sets of findings.

points.p: Loss of cortisol feedback raises ACTH
ACTH comes from POMC, shared with MSH
No aldosterone: less Na reabsorption, less K excretion in the distal nephron

prompts.q: Why does physiological stress cause an Addisonian crisis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: cortisol's job in the circulation.

points.p: Cortisol maintains vascular tone and catecholamine responsiveness
Stress needs a cortisol surge that fixed doses cannot make
Sick day rules mimic the surge

glossary.Addison's disease: Primary adrenal insufficiency: the adrenal cortex fails, so cortisol and aldosterone are lost.
glossary.Primary adrenal insufficiency: Adrenal failure from disease of the adrenal gland itself; ACTH is high.
glossary.Secondary adrenal insufficiency: Adrenal failure from low pituitary ACTH; no pigmentation and aldosterone is preserved.
glossary.Adrenal cortex: Outer layer of the adrenal gland that makes aldosterone, cortisol and androgens.
glossary.Zona glomerulosa: Outer cortical layer that makes aldosterone.
glossary.Zona fasciculata: Middle cortical layer that makes cortisol.
glossary.Cortisol: Main glucocorticoid; maintains blood pressure, glucose and the stress response.
glossary.Aldosterone: Mineralocorticoid that makes the kidney retain sodium and excrete potassium.
glossary.ACTH: Adrenocorticotropic hormone from the pituitary; drives cortisol production.
glossary.POMC: Pro-opiomelanocortin: the precursor protein cut into ACTH and MSH.
glossary.Hyperpigmentation: Darkening of the skin, e.g. palmar creases, scars and gums, from high ACTH.
glossary.Palmar creases: The lines on the palms; they darken in Addison's disease.
glossary.Buccal mucosa: The lining inside the cheeks; pigmented patches here suggest Addison's.
glossary.Vitiligo: Autoimmune loss of skin pigment in patches; associated with Addison's.
glossary.Autoimmune adrenalitis: Autoimmune destruction of the adrenal cortex; the commonest cause of Addison's in the UK.
glossary.21-hydroxylase: Adrenal enzyme; antibodies against it mark autoimmune Addison's.
glossary.Postural hypotension: A fall in blood pressure on standing, causing dizziness.
glossary.Addisonian crisis: Life-threatening acute adrenal insufficiency with shock, hypoglycaemia and hyperkalaemia.
glossary.Adrenal crisis: Acute, life-threatening cortisol deficiency needing immediate hydrocortisone.
glossary.Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome: Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage in meningococcal septicaemia, causing acute adrenal failure.
glossary.Meningococcal septicaemia: Bloodstream infection with Neisseria meningitidis, often with a non-blanching rash.
glossary.9am cortisol: Morning cortisol taken at its natural daily peak; the first test for adrenal insufficiency.
glossary.Short Synacthen test: Synthetic ACTH given, then cortisol measured at 30 minutes; confirms adrenal insufficiency.
glossary.Synacthen: Tetracosactide, a synthetic ACTH used in stimulation tests.
glossary.Diurnal: Following a daily rhythm; cortisol peaks in the morning and falls at night.
glossary.Renin: Kidney enzyme that drives the angiotensin-aldosterone system; high when aldosterone is low.
glossary.Hydrocortisone: Synthetic cortisol; the glucocorticoid replacement in Addison's.
glossary.Sick day rules: Doubling hydrocortisone during febrile illness to copy the normal stress cortisol surge.
glossary.Steroid emergency card: Card carried by steroid-dependent patients telling clinicians to give hydrocortisone in emergencies.
glossary.Conn's syndrome: Primary hyperaldosteronism: high sodium, low potassium and hypertension; the opposite of Addison's.
glossary.Distal nephron: The distal tubule and collecting duct, where aldosterone acts.
glossary.ENaC: Epithelial sodium channel in the collecting duct, increased by aldosterone.
glossary.Catecholamines: Adrenaline and noradrenaline; cortisol keeps blood vessels responsive to them.
glossary.SIADH: Syndrome of inappropriate ADH: euvolaemic hyponatraemia with normal potassium.
glossary.Hypopituitarism: Failure of the pituitary to make one or more hormones, including ACTH.

technique.stem: A 38 year old woman has a 3 month history of fatigue, weight loss and dizziness on standing. She craves salty food. She has type 1 diabetes. Her BP is 104/66 mmHg lying and 82/50 mmHg standing, pulse rate 96 bpm. Her palmar creases and buccal mucosa are pigmented.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: link the symptoms to the electrolytes and the skin.

clues: fatigue, weight loss and dizziness on standing
palmar creases and buccal mucosa are pigmented
steps.x: Postural hypotension, salt craving, pigmentation, hyperkalaemia and another autoimmune disease.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Addison's disease** (primary adrenal insufficiency).

elim: Anorexia does not cause pigmentation or hyperkalaemia.
Hypothyroidism causes weight gain, not pigmentation and postural hypotension.
Secondary insufficiency has low ACTH, so no pigmentation, and potassium is normal.
SIADH is euvolaemic with low sodium but normal potassium and no pigmentation.

steps.x: **A. Addison's disease.** Pigmentation + low Na + high K = primary adrenal failure.

technique.stem: A 45 year old man has a 2 month history of tiredness, nausea and weight loss. His BP is 108/68 mmHg. His 9am serum cortisol is 260 nmol/L (200–700). He is clinically stable.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate diagnostic investigation?

steps.x: It asks for the **diagnostic** test, so think dynamic testing.
Suspected adrenal insufficiency with a 9am cortisol in the 100–500 inconclusive range.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Short Synacthen test**.

elim: Imaging looks for a cause after the diagnosis is confirmed.
That tests for cortisol excess (Cushing's).
That screens for Conn's syndrome.
A grey-zone result needs a dynamic test now.

steps.x: **E. Short Synacthen test.** Cortisol 100–500 = do a short Synacthen test.

technique.stem: A 29 year old woman with Addison's disease has had diarrhoea and vomiting for 2 days and has not kept her tablets down. She is drowsy. Her temperature is 37.8°C, pulse rate 128 bpm, BP 74/40 mmHg, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Capillary glucose is 2.9 mmol/L.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

steps.x: Initial management of a collapsed Addison's patient.

clues: has not kept her tablets down
steps.x: Known Addison's, vomiting, shocked and hypoglycaemic: **adrenal crisis**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV** now, with 0.9% saline.

elim: She is vomiting and shocked; oral steroid will not be absorbed in time.
Fludrocortisone is oral only; high-dose hydrocortisone provides mineralocorticoid effect.
Hyperkalaemia improves with hydrocortisone and fluids; insulin would worsen her hypoglycaemia.
Never delay treatment for a test in crisis.

steps.x: **B. Hydrocortisone 100 mg IV.** Adrenal crisis = hydrocortisone 100 mg IV/IM immediately + saline.

technique.stem: A 41 year old man with newly diagnosed Addison's disease asks why his blood tests showed a high potassium.
technique.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Excess ACTH acting on the kidney
Reduced aldosterone-driven potassium secretion in the distal nephron

steps.x: A mechanism question: which missing hormone handles potassium?
Primary failure destroys the zona glomerulosa, so aldosterone falls.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Reduced aldosterone-driven K secretion in the distal nephron**.

elim: Cortisol loss does not cause haemolysis.
ACTH does not act on the nephron.
ADH affects sodium dilution, not potassium.
Insulin is not the problem here.

steps.x: **D. Reduced aldosterone-driven potassium secretion in the distal nephron.** No aldosterone = Na lost, K kept.

practice.stem: A 32 year old woman has a 4 month history of tiredness, weight loss and abdominal pain. She feels faint when she stands up. She has vitiligo. Her pulse rate is 98 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg lying and 80/50 mmHg standing. Her skin looks tanned, including her palmar creases.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Fatigue, weight loss, postural hypotension and palmar crease pigmentation with hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia is primary adrenal insufficiency. Hypopituitarism lowers ACTH so the skin is pale.

steps.x: Diagnosis: pigmentation plus electrolytes.

clues: feels faint when she stands up
steps.x: Postural hypotension, pigmentation, autoimmune history, low Na and high K.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Addison's disease**.

elim: Coeliac causes weight loss but not postural hypotension or hyperkalaemia.
Haemochromatosis pigments skin but causes diabetes and liver disease, not hyperkalaemia.
Hypopituitarism gives low ACTH, so pale skin and normal potassium.
Phaeochromocytoma causes paroxysmal hypertension.

steps.x: **A. Addison's disease.** Pigmentation + postural hypotension + low Na/high K = Addison's.

practice.stem: A 52 year old man with Addison's disease is brought in after collapsing at home. He has had a chest infection for 3 days and stopped taking his tablets because of vomiting. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 130 bpm, BP 72/40 mmHg and respiratory rate 26 breaths per minute. Capillary glucose is 2.6 mmol/L.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Shock, hypoglycaemia and hyperkalaemia in an Addison's patient who has missed steroids during an infection is an Addisonian crisis. Hypoglycaemia is common in crisis.

steps.x: Diagnosis in a collapsed patient with known Addison's.
Infection plus missed steroids; shock, hypoglycaemia, hyperkalaemia.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Addisonian (adrenal) crisis**.

elim: DKA has high glucose and ketones.
HHS has very high glucose.
Vomiting contributes, but missed steroids with hypoglycaemia and high K is adrenal crisis.
SIADH is euvolaemic, not shocked, with normal potassium.

steps.x: **A. Addisonian crisis.** Known Addison's + unwell + collapse = adrenal crisis.

practice.stem: A 30 year old woman with autoimmune hypothyroidism and vitiligo has primary adrenal insufficiency confirmed on a short Synacthen test. She has never taken steroids, has no history of tuberculosis and an adrenal CT shows small adrenal glands without calcification.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her adrenal insufficiency?
practice.e: Autoimmune adrenalitis causes 80 to 90% of Addison's disease and clusters with thyroid disease and vitiligo; it shrinks the glands. TB typically calcifies them.

steps.x: It asks for the cause of primary adrenal insufficiency.
Other autoimmune disease and small, uncalcified glands.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Autoimmune adrenalitis**.

elim: Metastases enlarge the glands, usually in older patients with cancer.
Amyloid is a rare infiltrative cause.
Haemorrhage is acute, with sepsis or anticoagulation.
TB gives enlarged or calcified adrenals; she has no TB history.

steps.x: **C. Autoimmune adrenalitis.** Most common cause (80–90%) = autoimmune; clusters with thyroid disease, vitiligo, T1DM.

practice.stem: A 36 year old woman has a 3 month history of fatigue, nausea and weight loss. She craves salt. Her pulse rate is 94 bpm and BP 98/60 mmHg lying and 82/52 mmHg standing. Her buccal mucosa is pigmented. Urea and electrolytes are sent.
practice.q: Which is the most likely result?
practice.e: Aldosterone deficiency in Addison's causes hyponatraemia and hyperkalaemia. High sodium with low potassium is Conn's syndrome.

steps.x: It asks which electrolytes fit the clinical picture.
Classic Addison's: aldosterone deficiency.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Low sodium, high potassium**.

elim: Low potassium suggests vomiting or diuretics, not aldosterone deficiency.
Normal results would not fit aldosterone loss.
High Na and low K is Conn's syndrome.
Hypernatraemia does not occur with aldosterone deficiency.

steps.x: **A. Sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 5.9 mmol/L.** Addison's = hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia; Conn's = the reverse.

practice.stem: A 40 year old man has a 6 month history of tiredness, weight loss and dizziness on standing. His sodium is 129 mmol/L and potassium 5.7 mmol/L. His pulse rate is 90 bpm and BP 104/64 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination?
practice.e: Primary adrenal insufficiency raises ACTH, which darkens palmar creases, scars and buccal mucosa. Pale skin fits secondary insufficiency, where ACTH is low.

steps.x: Most likely examination finding with this biochemistry.
Low Na, high K: aldosterone lost, so primary adrenal failure with high ACTH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Palmar crease pigmentation**.

elim: That suggests a pituitary tumour, which would cause secondary failure.
Exophthalmos is Graves' disease.
Pallor fits secondary (pituitary) insufficiency with low ACTH.
Striae are Cushing's (cortisol excess).

steps.x: **D. Pigmentation of the palmar creases.** Primary failure = high ACTH = pigmentation.

practice.stem: A 19 year old student has a 12 hour history of fever, headache and neck stiffness. She now has a spreading non-blanching purpuric rash. Her temperature is 39.6°C, pulse rate 140 bpm and BP 68/34 mmHg despite 2 litres of fluid. Her glucose is 2.7 mmol/L and potassium 6.0 mmol/L.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her refractory hypotension?
practice.e: Meningococcal septicaemia can cause bilateral adrenal haemorrhage (Waterhouse-Friderichsen syndrome), giving acute adrenal crisis with refractory shock, hypoglycaemia and hyperkalaemia.

steps.x: Why is the BP not responding? Look at glucose and potassium.

clues: glucose is 2.7 mmol/L and potassium 6.0 mmol/L
steps.x: Meningococcal septicaemia with hypoglycaemia and hyperkalaemia: acute adrenal failure.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage** (Waterhouse-Friderichsen).

elim: Anaphylaxis has urticaria and wheeze, not fever and purpura.
Tamponade gives raised JVP and muffled heart sounds.
There is no travel history.
Toxic shock gives a diffuse erythroderma, not purpura with hyperkalaemia.

steps.x: **B. Bilateral adrenal haemorrhage.** Meningococcal sepsis + refractory shock + high K, low glucose = Waterhouse-Friderichsen.

practice.stem: A 34 year old woman has a 3 month history of fatigue, weight loss and dizziness on standing. Her skin looks darker than usual. She is clinically stable. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 106/66 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: The initial test is a 9am cortisol, timed to the diurnal peak. A result of 100 to 500 nmol/L is inconclusive and needs a short Synacthen test.

steps.x: Initial test for suspected adrenal insufficiency in a stable patient.
Suspected Addison's, not in crisis.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **9am serum cortisol**.

elim: That screens for cortisol excess.
Imaging is for the cause, after diagnosis.
That is the screening test for Conn's.
Evening cortisol is naturally low and misleading.

steps.x: **B. 9am serum cortisol.** Initial = 9am cortisol; confirm = short Synacthen.

practice.stem: A 42 year old man with suspected Addison's disease has a short Synacthen test. He has hyperpigmentation, a sodium of 130 mmol/L and a potassium of 5.6 mmol/L.
practice.e: In Addison's the damaged cortex cannot respond to Synacthen, so cortisol fails to reach 450 nmol/L at 30 minutes. ACTH and renin are high in primary disease.

steps.x: It asks for the expected Synacthen result.
Primary failure: the adrenals cannot respond to synthetic ACTH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **30-minute cortisol below 450** (e.g. 210 nmol/L).

elim: A rise to 450 or more is a normal response.
ACTH is high in primary disease.
Renin is high because aldosterone is low.
That is a test for Cushing's.

steps.x: **A. 30-minute cortisol 210 nmol/L.** Pass = 30-minute cortisol ≥450 nmol/L; Addison's fails.

practice.stem: A 33 year old woman has just been diagnosed with autoimmune Addison's disease on a short Synacthen test. She has postural hypotension and a potassium of 5.6 mmol/L. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term management?
practice.e: Primary adrenal failure needs glucocorticoid replacement with hydrocortisone, mostly in the morning, and mineralocorticoid replacement with fludrocortisone.

steps.x: Long-term replacement in primary adrenal failure.
Both cortisol and aldosterone are missing.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone**.

elim: Night-time steroid disturbs sleep and the diurnal rhythm, and has no mineralocorticoid effect.
She also needs glucocorticoid replacement.
She is aldosterone deficient (postural hypotension, high K) and needs fludrocortisone too.
Spironolactone blocks aldosterone and would worsen hyperkalaemia.

steps.x: **D. Hydrocortisone and fludrocortisone.** Addison's = replace both: hydrocortisone (most in the morning) + fludrocortisone.

practice.stem: A 45 year old man with Addison's disease takes hydrocortisone 10 mg, 5 mg and 5 mg daily and fludrocortisone 100 micrograms daily. He has a flu-like illness with a temperature of 38.3°C. He is eating and drinking and not vomiting. His pulse rate is 96 bpm and BP 122/78 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate advice?
o: Go to the ED for IV hydrocortisone
Stop hydrocortisone until the fever settles
Use his IM hydrocortisone injection now
practice.e: Sick day rules: with a fever above 37.5°C, double the hydrocortisone dose and keep fludrocortisone the same. The IM kit is for vomiting.

steps.x: Sick day rules for a febrile but well patient.
Fever above 37.5°C, keeping tablets down.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **Double hydrocortisone, same fludrocortisone**.

elim: It is the other way round.
He is well, tolerating oral intake and not vomiting.
Stopping steroids risks crisis.
The injection is for vomiting or inability to take tablets.

steps.x: **B. Double hydrocortisone, same fludrocortisone.** Febrile >37.5°C = double hydrocortisone; vomiting = IM injection.

practice.stem: A 27 year old woman with Addison's disease has vomited 4 times in 3 hours with gastroenteritis and cannot keep her hydrocortisone down. She is at home and still alert. Her husband has her emergency kit.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate immediate action?
practice.e: If vomiting prevents oral steroids, the patient uses the IM hydrocortisone injection kit and continues until vomiting stops, seeking urgent medical help. Doubling tablets fails if they are not absorbed.

steps.x: Immediate action when vomiting stops oral steroids.
Vomiting = no steroid absorbed.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **IM hydrocortisone** from her kit, then seek medical help.

elim: Fludrocortisone is not increased and she cannot absorb it.
She cannot keep tablets down.
Fluids alone do not replace cortisol.
Delay risks adrenal crisis.

steps.x: **C. IM hydrocortisone injection.** Vomiting in Addison's = IM hydrocortisone, continue until vomiting stops.

practice.stem: A 37 year old woman with primary adrenal insufficiency has dark palmar creases and a pigmented scar. Her partner asks why her skin has darkened.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism?
o: Loss of cortisol feedback raising ACTH, which shares POMC with MSH
practice.e: Without cortisol negative feedback the pituitary makes excess ACTH from POMC, the same precursor as melanocyte-stimulating hormone, so the skin darkens. It does not occur in secondary disease.

steps.x: A mechanism question: why pigment in primary, not secondary, disease?
Primary failure: no cortisol feedback, high ACTH.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: **High ACTH from POMC, which also makes MSH**.

elim: Aldosterone is low and does not pigment skin.
That is haemochromatosis.
Cortisol has no direct pigment effect.
Palmar creases and scars are not sun-exposed sites.

steps.x: **C. Loss of cortisol feedback raising ACTH, which shares POMC with MSH.** Pigment = high ACTH = POMC = MSH.
